title: Connecting the Brain's Spark Plugs ⚡

mascot.name: Chip
mascot.greeting: Beep boop! Today we look inside your head. Your brain gave people the idea for a kind of AI called neural networks!

recap: A neuron is a tiny switch that says yes or no.
A weight says how much each clue counts.
A neuron learns by fixing its weights after each mistake.

sections.heading: 1. Meet the Neuron
sections.bigIdea: A neuron is a tiny switch that says yes or no.
sections.chipQuote: Your brain has billions of tiny cells. They help you see, think and move!

analogy.description: Think of a treasure box with two locks. It only opens when both keys turn. A neuron waits for enough clues before it says yes.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Your brain is full of **neurons**. Each one listens to clues from the cells next to it. When it gets enough clues, it switches on and sends a spark. If not, it stays quiet.

So a neuron is a bit like a light switch. It is on or off.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A tiny cell in your brain. It listens to clues and then says yes or no.

diagram.caption: How a neuron says yes or no
diagram.alt: Four steps: clues arrive at a neuron, the neuron adds them up, checks if it has enough, and then either sends a spark or stays quiet.
steps: Clues come in from other neurons. ✉️
The neuron adds up the clues. ➕
Enough? Spark! ⚡ Not enough? Stay quiet. 💤

more.title: The parts of a real neuron
more.bodyMarkdown: A real neuron has tiny branches called dendrites that catch signals. The middle of the cell adds them up. A long wire called an axon passes the signal on. Your brain has about 86 billion neurons!

teen.add: Scientists call switching on "firing". A neuron fires when its signals add up past a set level. Billions of these small choices, made at the same time, let you read this sentence.

checkIn.question: A neuron got enough clues. What does it do?
checkIn.praise: Yes! Enough clues means it switches on.
checkIn.explanation: A neuron switches on and sends a spark when it gets enough clues.

sections.heading: 2. Some Clues Count More
sections.bigIdea: Some clues matter more than others.
sections.chipQuote: Is it an apple? Let's look for clues!

analogy.description: A DJ has a slider for each sound. Push a slider up, and that sound gets loud. Pull it down, and it goes quiet.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
A neuron has a slider for each clue. We call it a **weight**. A big weight means the clue counts a lot. A small weight means it hardly counts.

To spot an apple, a sweet taste gets a big weight. A sticker on the skin gets no weight at all.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A number that says how much a clue counts. A big weight means a big say.

diagram.caption: Each clue has its own weight
diagram.content:
graph LR
    Sweet["🍬 Sweet? (big weight)"] -->|counts a lot| Add["➕ Add up the clues"]
    Round["⚪ Round? (some weight)"] -->|counts a bit| Add
    Sticker["🏷️ Sticker? (no weight)"] -.->|counts zero| Add
    Add --> Out{"🍎 Apple or not?"}
diagram.alt: Three clues go into an adder. Sweet has a big weight and counts a lot, round has some weight and counts a bit, and a sticker has no weight and counts zero. The adder then decides: apple or not?

teen.add: The neuron multiplies each clue by its weight and then adds up the results. This total is called the **weighted sum**.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: Each clue times its weight, all added together.

sections.heading: 3. Easy or Picky?
sections.bigIdea: Some neurons switch on easily. Some need lots of proof.
sections.chipQuote: One of my friends says yes to every game. Another one needs a lot of asking!

analogy.description: One friend says yes to every plan. Another friend says no until you give good reasons. A neuron can be easy or picky too.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
The **bias** sets how hard it is for the neuron to switch on. Change the bias, and the neuron gets easier or harder to switch on.

Weights and bias work as a team. Together they help the neuron make a good choice.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A number that makes a neuron easier or harder to switch on.

teen.add: In math, the bias is one more number added to the weighted sum. If the total ends up at zero or more, the neuron fires.

sections.heading: 4. A Neuron in a Computer
sections.bigIdea: A computer neuron learns by fixing its mistakes.
sections.chipQuote: When you learn to ride a bike, you wobble, fix it and try again!

analogy.description: You do not read a book to ride a bike. You wobble, you fix your balance, and you try again.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
People built a neuron out of math. It is called a **perceptron**. It looks at clues, adds them up and says yes or no.

At first it makes lots of mistakes. Each time it gets one wrong, it moves its weights a bit. After lots of practice, its guesses get good.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A neuron made of math inside a computer. It adds up clues and says yes or no.

more.title: Who built the first one?
more.bodyMarkdown: The first perceptron was built in 1957 by a scientist named Frank Rosenblatt. It was a big machine that learned to tell simple shapes apart.

teen.add: One perceptron can only learn simple rules. Put many of them in rows, and each row passes its answers to the next. These rows are called **layers**, and a stack of layers is a neural network.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A row of neurons that all get the same clues and pass their answers on to the next row.

checkIn.question: The perceptron got an answer wrong. What does it do next?
options: It moves its weights a bit
checkIn.praise: Right! Small fixes after each mistake are how it learns.
checkIn.explanation: After each mistake, the perceptron moves its weights a little, so its next guess is better.

sections.heading: 5. Train Your Own Neuron: The Fruit Sorter
sections.bigIdea: Now you get to teach a neuron!
sections.chipQuote: Move the sliders until the neuron can tell apples from lemons.

analogy.description: An apple is sweet and round. A lemon is sour and long. Help the neuron say apple for apples and lemon for lemons.

sections.bodyMarkdown: Pick a fruit. Then move the sliders and watch the total change. When the neuron gets it right, you have trained it!

interactiveWidget.title: ⚡ Try It: The Fruit Sorting Neuron
interactiveWidget.goal: Move the sliders so the neuron says apple for apples and lemon for lemons.
interactiveWidget.predictionPrompt: Before you start: which clue should count more, sweet or round?
hints: Give a bigger weight to the clue that tells the fruits apart.
Change the bias to make the neuron easier or harder to switch on.
interactiveWidget.successMessage: You trained a neuron! You moved the weights until it got the right answer.

miniQuiz.question: What does a weight do in a neuron?
options: It weighs the computer on a scale
It says how much a clue counts
miniQuiz.praise: Spot on! Weights tell the neuron which clues matter most.
miniQuiz.explanation: A big weight means a clue counts a lot. A small weight means it hardly counts.

miniQuiz.question: What does the bias change?
options: How hard it is for the neuron to switch on
miniQuiz.praise: Great! The bias makes a neuron easy or picky.
miniQuiz.explanation: Change the bias, and the neuron needs fewer or more clues before it says yes.

miniQuiz.question: What does a neuron do with its clues?
options: It adds them up and says yes or no
miniQuiz.praise: Yes! Add up the clues, then switch on or stay quiet.
miniQuiz.explanation: A neuron adds up its clues. If it has enough, it switches on.

miniQuiz.question: What do we call rows of neurons that pass their answers to the next row?
miniQuiz.praise: Exactly! Stack layers and you get a neural network.
miniQuiz.explanation: Neurons in a neural network sit in rows called layers. Each layer passes its answers to the next one.

teachBack.prompt: Chip asks: How does a neuron learn? Pick the best explanation for a friend.
options: It nudges its weights up or down until its guesses get better.
Someone types in the right answer every time.
teachBack.explanation: Yes! Learning means nudging the weights until the guesses are right.

recall.question: In a rule-based system, what does an if-then rule do?
options: Connects a fact to an action
recall.explanation: Rules link conditions to actions, so answers can be traced.
